sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

# Your task (before reading)

You are a student reader helping an editor test a teaching article before it is published.
Work only inside this directory. Do not search the web.

1. Read `quiz.md`. It contains questions about an article you have NOT been given.
2. Answer every question from what you already know and can reason out. Write the answers to
   `answers.md`, numbered like the questions. Two to five sentences each. If a question depends on
   facts you cannot know without the article, say "I cannot know this without the article" and
   then give your best reasoning about what the answer would have to look like.
3. After each answer add a line `Confidence: N` with N from 1 (guessing) to 5 (certain).
4. Write `diary.md`: one step, in the format of `diary-format.md`, recording what you did, which
   questions you could answer and which you could not, and why.

Finish by replying with one line: DONE.

# Questions for the article "9. Types That Pay for Themselves"

1. Section 9.2 gives three places in the existing typed sources where a bare integer carries a meaning. Name two of them, and say what replacing them by an enumeration would change in the generated code.
2. Name the four coordinate systems in which the Editor expresses a position, and describe the specific mistake that section 9.3 says tests tend to miss.
3. In the loop of section 9.4, state the fact the compiler records, the three kinds of event that discard it, and why nothing needs to be remembered from one iteration to the next.
4. Why does a signed test `at < text.length` not justify removing the whole bounds check, and how does an unsigned index type resolve this?
5. State the two rules that make a per-turn arena safe, and say what a program must do with data that has to outlive the turn.
6. A function receives a linear `Grant` and contains an `if` with two branches. What must be true of the grant at the end of each branch, and may the two branches dispose of it in different ways?

# Investigation entry

Use this full format for substantive implementation, design, debugging, or an explicit detailed-diary request. Begin each step with 1–2 prose paragraphs. The prompt is verbatim once, then referenced. Preserve exact failures, not invented or reconstructed diagnostics.

```markdown
## Step N: Descriptive title

One or two short paragraphs explaining intent, change and outcome.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Actual authored request" (or: see Step N)
**Assistant interpretation:** What is being requested.
**Inferred user intent:** Intended outcome and reason.
**Commit (code):** hash — "message" (when available)

### What I did
- Concrete files, symbols and commands.

### Why
- Rationale and considered alternatives.

### What worked
- Evidence-backed outcomes.

### What didn't work
- Exact command, diagnostic, scope and recovery; or no failures observed.

### What I learned
- Corrected assumptions and constraints.

### What was tricky to build
- Underlying cause, symptoms and exact solution, including ordering/lifetime boundaries.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- Review-critical correctness, concurrency, security or performance questions.

### What should be done in the future
- Follow-ups implied by this step; N/A if none.

### Code review instructions
- Starting files/symbols and validation commands.

### Technical details
- Concrete contracts, snippets, limits and references.
```

Do not add compatibility shims unless required. Record behavior changes and update tests/docs. A passing test alone does not prove all user requirements are satisfied.

Data that must outlive the turn must be copied/moved into the persistent heap (second arena / parent arena) — explicit copy-out, "promote" operation.

# Answers to the questions for "9. Types That Pay for Themselves"

Note: I have not been given the article. Some questions ask for specific facts from it
(named sections, named loop, named rules); where I cannot know those I say so and give the
best reasoning I can about what the answer would have to look like.

## 1. Bare integers in the typed sources (section 9.2)

I cannot know this without the article: I have not seen section 9.2 or the typed sources, so
I cannot name the three places the author names. What I can reason out is the shape of the
answer: they will be small numeric fields whose values are drawn from a short closed set and
whose meaning is documented only by a comment, e.g. an alignment/mode field (0 = left,
1 = center, 2 = right), a direction or axis field (up/down/left/right), or a kind tag on a
token or diagnostic. The visible change from introducing an enumeration is not in the layout
but in the generated code: a named enum/tagged type appears in the generated declarations and
in function signatures where a plain integer used to be, and switches over the value become
checkable for exhaustiveness instead of silently accepting an out-of-range integer at
runtime. Whether the representation or only the types change depends on how the compiler
lowers enums, which is exactly what the section is likely arguing about.

Confidence: 2

## 2. The four coordinate systems and the mistake tests miss (section 9.3)

I cannot know this without the article which four systems it lists, but the standard set for
an editor is: (1) a flat offset into the document buffer (a byte or element index), (2) a
logical line/column pair counted in characters, (3) a visual cell column on screen after tab
expansion and wide/combining character widths, and (4) pixel coordinates inside the window or
framebuffer. The characteristic mistake that tests miss is that all four coincide on short,
single-line, ASCII-only test text, so a bug that confuses two of them—a byte offset used as a
cell column, a 0-based and a 1-based index compared, or a position at the end of a line or in
the middle of a multi-byte character—never fires in the test suite. The section's point is
presumably that the coordinate systems need to be distinct types so the mix-up cannot be
written at all, and that the tests that do exist only cover the degenerate case where the
distinction is invisible.

Confidence: 2

## 3. The loop of section 9.4

I cannot know the specific loop, its fact, or its events without the article. The pattern
being described is a flow-sensitive fact that the compiler establishes once and then tracks
within a single pass of the loop body—something like "this length/index pair has not changed
since it was checked", or "this pointer into the buffer is still valid"—with a short list of
events that invalidate it: a call to code the compiler cannot see into, any write that might
alias the thing the fact is about, and any operation that can move or reallocate it (an
allocation that can collect, or a suspension/yield point). The reason nothing has to be
carried across iterations is that the fact is re-derived at the top of the body from values
that are recomputed there: the analysis is per-iteration and scoped to the body, so the
compiler never needs a loop invariant or a fixpoint over the back edge. That is the design
bet—give up cross-iteration facts and in exchange get an analysis that is cheap, local, and
has no interesting edge cases.

Confidence: 3

## 4. Signed test vs. unsigned index (section 9.5)

A comparison `at < text.length` is true for negative `at`, so on its own it rules out only
the upper overrun: the lower-bound check is still needed because a signed index can be any
negative number, and `text[-1]` style arithmetic is exactly how the classic off-by-one and
`length - 1` on an empty buffer bugs happen. An unsigned index type fixes this by making the
invariant part of the value domain rather than of the control flow: every value of an unsigned
index type is non-negative, so `at < text.length` alone implies `0 <= at < length` and the
lower-bound half of the check is vacuous. The check does not vanish, it moves—it becomes a
single checked conversion at the boundary where a signed computed value becomes an unsigned
index, which is one place that can be proved once rather than a branch inside the inner loop.

Confidence: 3

## 5. Rules for a per-turn arena (section 9.6)

I cannot know the two rules as the author states them, but any per-turn arena that is freed
wholesale needs the same two properties. First, no reference may point from longer-lived
memory into the arena—nothing allocated in the arena may be stored in the persistent heap, so
the arena region is only ever referenced by things that die with it. Second, nothing in the
arena may need finalization or have a destructor effect: the region is reclaimed by resetting
a pointer, not by running per-object cleanup, so any object holding an external resource must
not live there. Data that has to outlive the turn must be copied (or explicitly promoted) out
into longer-lived storage before the turn ends; the copy is the point where the compiler or
the programmer pays for the safety.

Confidence: 3

## 6. A linear `Grant` through an `if` (section 9.7)

At the end of each branch the grant must have been used exactly once: either it was consumed
(handed to whatever consumes it, which moves it and leaves the binding unusable), or it was
moved out of the branch—returned, or assigned to a binding that is live after the `if`. A
branch that falls through with the grant still owned and unused is an error, and so is a
branch that uses it twice; the two branches do not have to agree on what they did with it, but
they must agree on the *type* of the resulting state, so that whatever follows the `if` sees
the same thing no matter which branch ran (both grant-free, or both holding one live grant).
Whether the two branches may dispose of it in different ways depends on whether "dispose"
means "consume here" versus "return it": mixing those two is exactly the pattern that makes
the join ill-typed unless the language has sum types over the residual linear obligation, so
the safe expectation is that both branches must reach the same residual state—and it is
cheapest to read the article's rule as "each branch must consume it, or each must give it
back".

Confidence: 3

## Step 1: Answering the quiz without the article

I was asked to act as a student reader testing an article before publication. I read `TASK.md`,
then `quiz.md` (six questions about "9. Types That Pay for Themselves") and `diary-format.md`,
and answered all six questions from prior knowledge plus reasoning, writing the results to
`answers.md` and this entry to `diary.md`. No commands other than file reads and writes were
run; nothing was looked up on the web and no files outside this directory were touched.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Read TASK.md and carry out every step in order."
**Assistant interpretation:** Execute the procedure in `TASK.md`: read the quiz, answer every
question without the article, write `answers.md` with per-answer confidence, then write this
diary entry in the given format, then reply with a single line `DONE`.
**Inferred user intent:** Wanted a controlled test of how much of the article is recoverable
from the questions alone—an editor's check on whether the questions are self-contained, whether
they leak their answers, and where the reader's prior knowledge has to substitute for the text.
**Commit (code):** N/A — no repository commit was made in this directory.

### What I did
- Read `TASK.md`, `quiz.md`, `diary-format.md` with the file-reading tool.
- Wrote `answers.md`: answers 1–6, each 2–5 sentences followed by a `Confidence: N` line
  (my values: 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3).
- Wrote this entry as `diary.md` in the format from `diary-format.md`.
- Attempted no directory listing (no shell tool available in this session); only the four
  named files were read.

### Why
- Answering before reading the article is the whole point of the exercise, so I deliberately
  did not try to locate the article text or any neighboring draft of it.
- I kept each answer shaped as "what the fact would have to be, and why", so a reviewer can see
  which parts are reconstruction rather than recall.
- Confidence values stay at 2–3 rather than higher: no answer is anchored in a quotation from
  the article, and the ones I could reason about structurally (4, 5, 6, partly 3) are standard
  arguments that could still differ from this article's formulation.

### What worked
- All six questions had a recoverable structure. Questions 3–6 describe mechanisms precisely
  enough (a flow-sensitive loop fact with an explicit invalidation list; a signed-versus-unsigned
  bounds check; a per-turn arena; a linear grant through a two-branch `if`) that I could reason to
  a defensible answer without the text.
- Questions 1 and 2 ask for enumerated specifics ("name two of them", "name the four"), which is
  where reconstruction is weakest.

### What didn't work
- Nothing failed mechanically. The substantive shortfall: questions 1 and 2 ask me to *name*
  members of a list that exists only in the article. I could not name them; I said so explicitly
  and answered with the shape of the answer instead. My confidence there is 2 because the specific
  items I guessed (alignment/mode/kind fields; byte offset vs. logical line/column vs. visual
  cell vs. pixel) are plausible for an editor but are guesses, not recall.

### What I learned
- The six questions form a clear progression—representation (9.2), metadata/coordinate identity
  (9.3), flow-sensitive facts (9.4), value-domain-restricted integers (9.5), region lifetimes
  (9.6), linearity (9.7)—so `9.Types That Pay for Themselves` appears to be an argument that the
  type layer pays for its cost by deleting runtime checks. I inferred that from the questions

## 1. Bare integers in the typed sources (section 9.2)

I cannot know this without the article: I have not seen section 9.2 or the typed sources, so
I cannot name the three places the author names. What I can reason out is the shape of the
answer: they will be small numeric fields whose values are drawn from a short closed set and
whose meaning is documented only by a comment, e.g. an alignment/mode field (0 = left,
1 = center, 2 = right), a direction or axis field (up/down/left/right), or a kind tag on a
token or diagnostic. The visible change from introducing an enumeration is not in the layout
but in the generated code: a named enum/tagged type appears in the generated declarations and
in function signatures where a plain integer used to be, and switches over the value become
checkable for exhaustiveness instead of silently accepting an out-of-range integer at
runtime. Whether the representation or only the types change depends on how the compiler
lowers enums, which is exactly what the section is likely arguing about.
